KV cache fragmentation in continuous batching inference servers arises because the memory required to store a sequence's key-value tensors grows dynamically as tokens are generated, yet the allocator must commit physical blocks before knowing the final sequence length — creating a tension between reservation granularity and actual occupancy. The central question is: given a preemptive scheduler that can evict and later resume sequences, how do you allocate, track, and reclaim KV cache memory across heterogeneous concurrent sequences without either stranding large contiguous holes (external fragmentation) or wasting space within allocated blocks (internal fragmentation)? The concepts that matter are block-granular allocation (as in vLLM's PagedAttention, where logical KV pages map to non-contiguous physical blocks), preemption policies (swap-to-CPU vs. recomputation-on-resume), and the interaction between sequence length distribution and block size — a large block size amortizes metadata overhead but amplifies internal fragmentation for short sequences. What a beginner misses is that fragmentation here is not a static property of the allocator but a dynamic function of the scheduler's decisions: aggressive preemption of long sequences frees large contiguous physical blocks but imposes resume latency, while tolerating partial completion wastes blocks that are logically "claimed" by sequences that may never finish. Experts also worry about the correlation structure of request length distributions — if the arriving workload contains a fat tail of very long sequences interleaved with short ones, no fixed block size is Pareto-optimal, and runtime block coalescing becomes necessary but introduces its own synchronization overhead during attention kernel execution.

The cost boundary between recomputation and CPU swap is determined by three interacting quantities: the number of tokens already processed (which sets recomputation FLOP cost as roughly proportional to sequence length squared for full attention, or linear for chunked prefill), the PCIe bandwidth available for host-device transfer (typically 16–32 GB/s on PCIe 4.0/5.0), and the size of the KV cache blocks being evicted (each token's KV entry is 2 × num_layers × num_heads × head_dim × dtype_bytes — for LLaMA-3 70B in fp16 that's roughly 640 KB per token across all layers). Recomputation wins when sequences are short enough that re-prefilling them costs less GPU time than the PCIe round-trip latency plus the opportunity cost of blocking the decode stream during swap-in; empirically this crossover often falls around 512–1024 tokens under moderate load, a figure vLLM's original Soejima et al. (2023) paper implicitly acknowledges by defaulting to recomputation for short evictions. The boundary is not fixed but shifts with the ratio of active concurrent sequences to available CPU memory bandwidth: under high-concurrency regimes, many sequences compete for the same PCIe channel simultaneously, serializing swap-ins and inflating effective transfer latency far beyond the raw bandwidth figure — a convoy effect that can push the crossover point toward much longer sequences where recomputation would otherwise lose. Simultaneously, high concurrency means the GPU is rarely idle during a recomputation prefill, so the "free" GPU cycles assumption breaks down and recomputation now directly steals capacity from live decode batches, increasing per-token latency for all concurrent users. Systems like DejaVu (2023) and DistServe attack this from the disaggregation angle — separating prefill and decode onto different GPU pools so recomputation cost doesn't contaminate decode throughput — but this introduces cross-node KV transfer overhead that must itself be weighed against local swap cost. The practical implication is that no static policy is optimal: production systems like TensorRT-LLM's scheduler use heuristics conditioned on current queue depth and sequence length histograms to switch between strategies dynamically, though the optimal switching threshold remains an open empirical question.

Partial eviction creates a layer-boundary coherence problem: during resume, the attention kernel for layer L expects its KV tensors to reflect the token state at the exact prefill checkpoint, but if layers 0–15 were swapped to CPU and layers 16–31 were retained on GPU, the resume must interleave PCIe transfers with GPU-side forward passes — and any scheduling slip that allows a concurrent sequence to overwrite the retained GPU blocks (due to the allocator reclaiming "idle" memory) invalidates the retained layers silently, with no checksum or generation counter to detect the corruption. The deeper consistency issue is that most block allocators, including vLLM's, treat eviction as an atomic per-sequence decision precisely to avoid this state: the reference-counted PagedAttention block table has no sub-sequence or per-layer granularity, so partial eviction requires either extending the metadata schema (adding a per-layer eviction bitmap per logical block) or falling back to full eviction, both of which current open-source implementations avoid entirely. When partial eviction is attempted naively — as some research prototypes do by evicting only the top-K most memory-intensive layers — the resume logic must reconstruct the missing layers by running a partial forward pass from the last fully retained layer, which requires storing intermediate activations at layer boundaries as re-entry points; these activation checkpoints are not the same as KV cache entries and consume additional memory that most inference servers have no allocator path to manage. Coherence also breaks under tensor parallelism: in a TP=4 configuration, each GPU holds a shard of every KV layer, so "partial eviction" of layer 16 means evicting four coordinated shards atomically across four devices — if one shard swap lags due to NUMA asymmetry or PCIe contention, the resume barrier must stall all four ranks, and current NCCL-based synchronization has no fine-grained "shard-ready" signaling primitive to express this efficiently. Systems like Infinite-LLM (2024) and its disaggregated KV store approach move toward treating KV blocks as independently addressable objects in a distributed cache, which is a necessary precondition for safe partial eviction, but they still operate at sequence granularity for consistency boundaries rather than layer granularity. The failure mode that practitioners actually encounter is more mundane but pernicious: partial eviction under memory pressure causes the attention kernel to silently read stale GPU-resident blocks for retained layers while loading refreshed CPU blocks for evicted layers, producing outputs with anomalous perplexity spikes that are nearly impossible to attribute to cache coherence rather than model or quantization error without layer-level logging instrumentation that no production system currently exposes.

In vLLM's prefix-sharing implementation, a physical block with reference count > 1 is copy-on-write protected and cannot be evicted while any referencing sequence is active — but this protection dissolves the moment all referencing sequences are preempted simultaneously, at which point the block's refcount drops to zero and the allocator treats it as freely reclaimable, losing the shared prefix silently without notifying any of the suspended sequences that their logical block table entries now point to reclaimed memory. The ownership problem is structurally unresolved: when multiple preempted sequences share a prefix block and one is scheduled for resumption first, the resuming sequence must reload the prefix, but the block allocator has no mechanism to re-establish the shared mapping — it allocates a fresh private block for the resuming sequence and the subsequently resumed sequences each get their own independent reload, multiplying PCIe transfer cost by the number of sharers rather than paying it once. This "ownership vacuum" means the system silently degrades from O(1) prefix sharing to O(N) redundant reloads under preemption pressure, and because the block table is rebuilt from scratch per sequence during resume rather than being reconstructed from a persistent prefix registry, there is no hook to detect that two resuming sequences could share a freshly reloaded block. The consistency semantics break in a subtler way under chunked prefill with partial eviction: if a shared prefix block was partially filled (its last few slots occupied by the tail of the prompt rather than a clean block boundary), evicting it invalidates a non-power-of-two token span that the resuming sequence must recompute, but the recomputed tokens may hash differently if any positional encoding is absorbed into the KV projection — meaning the "same" prefix produces a different KV tensor depending on whether it was computed in one pass or split across a preemption boundary. RadixAttention (SGLang, 2024) improves prefix reuse under normal operation by organizing shared blocks into a radix tree with LRU eviction at the node level, but its eviction policy still treats each node as atomic and provides no ownership transfer protocol for the multi-sequence resume case, meaning the same redundant reload problem persists under concurrent preemption. The fundamental issue is that reference counting as implemented in these systems tracks liveness but not resumption responsibility — what is needed is a lease or epoch mechanism where one designated sequence holds a "reload lease" on each shared block, and other sequences sharing that block register as dependents that inherit the reloaded physical address rather than triggering independent transfers, a primitive that does not exist in any current open-source inference server.

A lease holder preempted mid-reload creates a classic livelock-adjacent condition: the scheduler evicts the lease holder because memory pressure has not abated (the reload itself is consuming PCIe bandwidth and temporary double-buffering space), but evicting the lease holder orphans the in-flight DMA transfer — the CPU-side pinned buffer is still being written while the GPU-side destination block is reclaimed, and unless the allocator has explicit "transfer-in-flight" block state (distinct from "occupied" and "free"), the physical block can be reassigned to a new sequence whose KV writes race with the completing DMA engine. The deadlock scenario emerges when dependent sequences cannot be scheduled without the shared prefix (their logical block tables are invalid until the lease holder completes reload), the lease holder cannot complete reload without GPU memory to land the transferred blocks, and no GPU memory can be freed without scheduling one of the dependent sequences to completion — a three-way circular wait that no current inference scheduler has preemption priority logic to break because schedulers like vLLM's treat memory availability as a precondition for scheduling rather than a resource that scheduling decisions themselves affect. Livelock is arguably more likely than true deadlock in practice: the scheduler repeatedly selects the lease holder for resumption, begins the PCIe transfer, detects memory pressure from concurrent sequences, preempts the lease holder again, and cancels or abandons the partial transfer — each cycle consuming PCIe bandwidth and pinned CPU buffer allocation without making forward progress, analogous to the "thrashing" regime in virtual memory systems under insufficient physical RAM. The interaction with lease expiry timers makes this worse: if leases expire after a fixed wall-clock interval (the natural choice to bound dependent-sequence starvation), an expired lease triggers lease reassignment to another dependent sequence, which must restart the reload from scratch — but if that new lease holder is also vulnerable to preemption for the same memory pressure reasons, the system can cycle through all dependent sequences without any completing, a starvation cascade with period proportional to PCIe transfer time times number of dependents. Operating systems literature has solved analogous problems via priority inheritance (the lease holder inherits the maximum priority of all dependent sequences, making preemption of an active reload prohibitively expensive to the scheduler) and non-preemptible critical sections for short memory operations, but inference schedulers couple memory allocation and compute scheduling so tightly that implementing priority inheritance would require exposing sequence dependency graphs to the scheduler — a architectural separation that systems like Sarathi-Serve (2024) approach for chunked prefill pipelining but do not extend to KV cache reload coordination. The cleanest resolution would be to make reload an atomic, non-preemptible micro-transaction with a memory reservation made before the lease is granted — essentially guaranteeing that the destination physical blocks are locked against reclamation for the duration of the PCIe transfer — but this requires the allocator to support a "reserved-pending" state and the scheduler to account for reserved-but-empty blocks when computing available memory, a two-phase commit over memory that adds coordination overhead on every allocation decision.

Expressing reload leases as a first-class scheduling primitive requires the scheduler to maintain a dependency DAG over sequences rather than the flat priority queue that vLLM and Sarathi-Serve currently use — each lease holder becomes a DAG node with weighted edges to its dependents, and the scheduler's selection policy must treat the subgraph rooted at a lease holder as an atomic scheduling unit whose collective memory footprint and expected completion time are evaluated jointly rather than per-sequence. The objective function must simultaneously minimize time-to-first-token for new requests, maximize decode throughput for active sequences, and minimize lease holder preemption probability — three objectives that are not jointly convex, since reducing lease holder preemption probability requires reserving memory blocks early (increasing memory pressure on decode batches) while maximizing decode throughput requires maximizing batch size (consuming exactly that reserved memory). A tractable formulation is to express this as a constrained optimization: maximize aggregate decode token throughput subject to the constraint that no lease holder's reload is preempted more than K times before completion, with K as a tunable parameter — this converts the multi-objective problem into a single-objective with a soft priority floor, analogous to the "max-min fairness with priority classes" formulations used in cluster schedulers like Themis (NSDI 2020) but applied at the memory-block granularity rather than GPU-job granularity. Priority inversion at scale emerges when many lease holders simultaneously hold reservations: if 32 sequences each hold a 4-block reservation for pending reloads, 128 blocks are effectively removed from the allocator's free pool, and the scheduler's memory availability estimate diverges from physical reality by exactly that margin — causing it to admit new sequences it cannot actually serve, which then trigger further preemptions, which create further lease holders, in a feedback loop that resembles the TCP incast problem in congestion control. The most promising practical architecture is a two-level scheduler: an outer level that manages lease grants, reservations, and dependency tracking on a coarse time horizon (tens of milliseconds), and an inner level that handles chunk-level interleaving and batch composition at the microsecond scale — separating policy from mechanism in a way that allows the outer scheduler to implement priority inheritance and reservation accounting without adding latency to the inner decode loop, a decomposition that neither vLLM nor any current open-source system has implemented.

Speculative decoding rejection invalidates KV cache blocks in a way that is structurally different from preemption-driven eviction: when the target model rejects draft tokens at position k, all KV blocks written for positions k through k+γ (where γ is the speculation depth, typically 4–8 tokens) must be discarded and rewritten with the corrected token's KV entries, but if any lease-dependent sequence had registered a sharing intent on those blocks — expecting to inherit a prefix ending at position k+γ — the dependency DAG now contains edges pointing to physically invalid blocks whose logical addresses have not yet been updated. The ripple is asymmetric: the lease holder's block table is corrected synchronously during the verification step, but the dependent sequences' logical block tables are not automatically invalidated because the DAG edge encodes "will share block B" rather than "currently shares block B," and no current system performs a DAG traversal on every speculative rejection to push invalidation notifications to dependents — meaning dependents can be scheduled for resumption with stale block table entries that point to blocks now containing corrected-token KV data from a different sequence position. The severity scales with speculation depth and acceptance rate: at a 70% token acceptance rate (typical for well-matched draft-target pairs on coding tasks per the SpecInfer paper, 2023), roughly 30% of speculated blocks are invalidated per step, and with γ=8 this means an average of 2.4 blocks per sequence per decoding step experience content replacement — if 16 sequences share a common prefix in the speculation window, each rejection event potentially triggers 16 DAG edge invalidations that must be processed before the next scheduling decision. A subtle coherence failure arises specifically when the rejected position falls within a shared prefix block rather than a sequence-private block: the block's physical content is overwritten with corrected KV entries, its logical identity in the prefix tree (RadixAttention's trie or equivalent) must be updated, and any dependent sequence that already copied the block's physical address into its own block table now has a valid physical pointer to a block whose semantic content has changed underneath it — a use-after-semantic-change bug that is invisible to reference counting because the block was never freed. Systems like Medusa (2024) and EAGLE avoid some of this by keeping speculative KV writes in a separate staging buffer that is only committed to the main cache upon acceptance, which is precisely the right architectural boundary — but staging buffers interact poorly with the reservation mechanism because reserved blocks in the main cache cannot be filled from staging until acceptance, extending the window during which dependent sequences are blocked and increasing the probability that their leases expire before the prefix materializes. The cleanest DAG-aware fix is to attach a "speculative epoch" tag to every block written during a speculation window, and to require that DAG edges declare whether they depend on committed or speculative blocks — allowing the scheduler to defer dependent sequence resumption until epoch commitment, at the cost of adding epoch tracking to the block allocator and a commit/abort protocol to the verification step, neither of which exists in any current open-source speculative decoding implementation.

When the main cache lacks free blocks at commit time, the system faces a forced choice between three options, all bad: block the verification step until eviction frees enough space (stalling the entire decode batch since verification and decode share the same CUDA stream in most implementations), abort the speculative tokens and fall back to single-token decode (discarding the throughput gain that motivated speculation in the first place), or commit partially by accepting only the tokens whose KV blocks fit and treating the remainder as rejected (which is semantically invalid since partial acceptance at a non-rejection boundary produces an inconsistent KV state). The back-pressure on the in-flight decode batch is particularly damaging because speculative decoding's latency advantage depends on amortizing verification cost across γ accepted tokens — if commit failure forces single-token fallback, the verification FLOP cost was paid in full but yields only one token, inverting the efficiency argument and making speculative decoding strictly worse than standard decoding for that step, a failure mode that compounds if memory pressure is sustained across multiple steps. The interaction with the in-flight batch is a CUDA stream synchronization problem: in systems like TensorRT-LLM that pipeline verification and the next prefill chunk on overlapping streams, a commit stall on stream A must insert a synchronization barrier that also blocks stream B's prefill chunk from accessing blocks that might be evicted to satisfy the commit — effectively serializing two operations that were designed to overlap, collapsing pipeline utilization to the sequential case. Memory pressure at commit time is more likely than it appears because staging buffers themselves consume GPU memory that the allocator typically does not account for in its free-block estimates: if γ=8 and batch size is 64, up to 512 blocks are simultaneously staged, and a naive allocator that sizes admission decisions against main-cache free blocks without subtracting staged capacity will systematically overcommit, guaranteeing commit failures under any sustained load above roughly (1 - γ×block_size/total_cache) utilization. EAGLE-2 (2024) partially addresses this by dynamically adjusting speculation depth based on estimated acceptance rate, which indirectly reduces staging pressure, but it does not model main-cache commit capacity as a constraint in its depth selection policy — meaning it can still generate staging pressure that exceeds commit capacity at high batch sizes even with reduced γ. The correct fix requires the allocator to maintain a "committed high-water mark" that reserves enough free blocks to absorb one full speculation window before each decode step begins, effectively treating staged-block commit capacity as a first-class resource alongside free blocks and reserved-pending blocks — a three-way allocator state that would allow the scheduler to preemptively evict low-priority sequences before staging begins rather than discovering the shortage at commit time when the decode batch is already mid-flight.
